+def _apply_table(s, table):
+    """
+    Apply a _replace_table to the str s. A merge whose two tokens are not both
+    in s cannot match, so its scan is skipped: present holds every code point
+    of s (the initial ones plus each token a replace minted; tokens merged
+    away are kept, which only means a scan that finds nothing).
+    """
+    present = set(s)
+    replace = s.replace
+    n = len(s)
+    for ps, a, b, c in table:
+        if a in present and b in present:
+            s = replace(ps, c)
+            m = len(s)
+            if m != n:
+                n = m
+                present.add(c)
+                replace = s.replace
+    return s

actions.reason: My one change made encode slower. It skipped str.replace scans for merges whose tokens are not in the string, using a set of the characters present. The sandbox rejected it: encode_ir ratio 1.0076 and train_ir 1.0017. Outputs were identical, so the problem was speed, not correctness. The replace loop does not seem to be where encode time goes; startup, imports and benchmark overhead probably dominate. I reverted the edits to basic.py and regex.py. One leftover: I accidentally created an empty file, minbpe/basic.py.tmp_unused. Nothing imports it, but my tools can't delete it, so it needs removing by hand. I have no candidate to submit.

journal.text:
I tried to speed up encode in minbpe by skipping str.replace scans for merges whose tokens cannot appear in the string. I tracked the set of characters present and skipped any merge that used a missing one. The edits touched minbpe/basic.py and minbpe/regex.py, and I reverted a larger 26-line addition in basic.py before evaluating.

The sandbox rejected it as no_improvement. encode_ir went from 408790090 to 411882558, a ratio of 1.0076 against a required 0.9900. train_ir went from 359361609 to 359966704, a ratio of 1.0017. Outputs were identical and the guard passed, so this was a speed problem, not a correctness one. I submitted no candidate.

I now think the replace loop is not where encode instructions go. The cost of keeping the character set outweighs the scans it saves. My guess is that startup, imports and benchmark overhead dominate, but I have not measured that.

Next time I should profile the encode_ir path in lineage_bench.py before editing, and only touch the replace table once the profile shows it is hot.
